# Casual Office

> Casual Office is an open-source, self-hosted office suite for working with native Microsoft Office documents in the browser. It includes spreadsheet, document, presentation, desktop, collaboration, and file management applications built around open file formats and real-time collaboration. It also develops the embeddable Rust engines underneath those applications (OpenCalc for spreadsheets, OpenDoc for documents) and Enclave, a self-hostable enterprise content and governance platform.

## Project

* Website: https://casualoffice.org
* GitHub: https://github.com/CasualOffice
* License: Apache-2.0 (some components include preserved MIT attribution where required)
* Author: Sachin Sarwa

## Products

### Casual Sheets

Open-source spreadsheet editor with native `.xlsx` support, real-time collaboration, and self-hosted deployment.

* Repository: https://github.com/CasualOffice/sheets
* Documentation: https://casualoffice.org/docs/sheets/
* Live Demo: https://sheet.casualoffice.org/

### Casual Docs

Open-source `.docx` editor focused on high-fidelity editing and real-time collaboration.

* Repository: https://github.com/CasualOffice/docs
* Documentation: https://casualoffice.org/docs/editor/
* Live Demo: https://docs.casualoffice.org/

### Casual Slides

Open-source presentation editor for native `.pptx` files.

* Repository: https://github.com/CasualOffice/slides
* Overview: https://casualoffice.org/casual-slides/
* Live Demo: none yet — ships with v0.1.0

### Casual PDF

Open-source, high-fidelity PDF viewer and editor: annotate, fill forms, edit text in place, e-sign (PKCS#7 certified signing), and perform true byte-level redaction. One PDFium engine is shared across web and desktop for identical fidelity.

* Documentation: https://casualoffice.org/casual-pdf/
* Live Demo: https://pdf.casualoffice.org/

### Casual Desktop

Desktop application built with Tauri that reuses the web editors for offline editing. Includes an on-device agentic AI assistant (plan, edit, review) that runs a local model so documents never leave the machine.

* Repository: https://github.com/CasualOffice/desktop
* Downloads: https://casualoffice.org/casual-desktop/

## Engines

The engines are a second generation: ground-up Rust rewrites of the spreadsheet and document
cores, designed to be embedded rather than deployed. Both are developed in the open alongside
the applications above. They are NOT yet drop-in replacements for Casual Sheets and Casual Docs,
which are what the live application demos run today.

### OpenCalc

An embeddable spreadsheet engine written in Rust. Reads and writes `.xlsx` (plus CSV/TSV/PSV),
calculates 347 of the 356 spec functions including `LET`, `LAMBDA` and dynamic arrays, and
renders a canvas grid. The whole engine runs client-side as WebAssembly, so co-editing scales
without sticky sessions. Successor to Casual Sheets. Status: alpha; npm SDK published at 0.0.0.

* Repository: https://github.com/CasualOffice/opencalc
* Overview: https://casualoffice.org/opencalc/
* Project site: https://calc.casualoffice.org/
* Live editor: https://calc.casualoffice.org/editor.html
* npm: `@opencalc/sheet`, `@opencalc/react`, `@opencalc/engine`

### OpenDoc

A deterministic, embeddable Word-document engine written in Rust. Reads and writes `.docx`,
holds the document in a normalized editable model, and lays it out and renders it to pixels for
native, WebAssembly, and headless hosts — without a browser, a server, or a UI framework.
Successor to Casual Docs. Status: pre-release; no published package line yet.

* Repository: https://github.com/CasualOffice/opendoc
* Overview: https://casualoffice.org/opendoc/
* Project site: https://opendoc.casualoffice.org/
* Live editor: https://opendoc.casualoffice.org/editor.html

## Platform

### Enclave

A self-hostable enterprise content and collaboration platform — SharePoint-class in purpose.
Workspaces, libraries and immutable versions; local/LDAP/OIDC/SAML/SCIM identity; granular
per-action permissions with deny-wins ACL resolution; DLP, classification, information barriers,
retention, records, legal hold and tamper-evident audit; permission-aware hybrid search over
Milvus; and an MCP gateway so AI access runs through the same policy chain as every other entry
point. Rust + Axum + PostgreSQL on the back, React + TypeScript on the front.
Status: in development — specification complete, implementation underway, no hosted demo.

* Repository: https://github.com/CasualOffice/enclave
* Overview: https://casualoffice.org/enclave/

## Other components

### Casual Drive

Self-hosted file manager for Office documents with browser-based editing.

* Repository: https://github.com/CasualOffice/drive

### Casual Collab

Real-time collaboration server based on Yjs and Hocuspocus.

* Repository: https://github.com/CasualOffice/collab

## Core Principles

* Open source and self-hostable.
* Native Office file formats are the primary document format.
* Real-time collaboration without vendor lock-in.
* Standards-based architecture.
* Browser, desktop, and self-hosted deployments.
* Docker-first deployment.

## Technology

Casual Office is primarily built with:

* TypeScript
* React
* Rust
* Go
* Tauri
* Docker
* Yjs
* Hocuspocus
* Univer OSS
* ProseMirror
* WebAssembly (wasm32-unknown-unknown)
* PostgreSQL
* Milvus
* Model Context Protocol (MCP)

## Common Questions

Q: What is Casual Office?
A: An open-source, self-hosted office suite for editing native Microsoft Office documents — spreadsheets (.xlsx), documents (.docx), presentations (.pptx), and PDFs — directly in the browser, with real-time collaboration. It is a self-hostable alternative to Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, and OnlyOffice.

Q: Is Casual Office free and open source?
A: Yes. It is licensed under Apache-2.0 (some components preserve MIT attribution where required) and can be self-hosted at no cost.

Q: What file formats does it support?
A: Native Office formats are the primary formats: .xlsx / .ods / .csv / .tsv (Sheets), .docx (Docs), .pptx (Slides), and PDF (Casual PDF). Files round-trip in their original format rather than being converted to a proprietary one.

Q: Can I self-host it?
A: Yes. Deployment is Docker-first, with self-host storage options including memory, local disk, S3, and Postgres. See the documentation for self-hosting guides.

Q: Does it support real-time collaboration?
A: Yes. Co-editing is powered by Yjs and the Hocuspocus/Casual Collab server, so multiple users can edit the same document simultaneously without vendor lock-in.

Q: What is the difference between Casual Sheets and OpenCalc, or Casual Docs and OpenDoc?
A: They are two generations of the same job. Casual Sheets and Casual Docs are the shipping web applications (TypeScript/Univer and ProseMirror respectively) and are what the live demos run today. OpenCalc and OpenDoc are their successors: deterministic Rust engines that compile to WebAssembly and embed into any host — browser, native, or headless — without a DOM, a server, or a UI framework. Do not describe the engines as replacements for the applications; both generations exist and are developed in the open.

Q: What is Enclave?
A: Enclave is a self-hostable enterprise content and collaboration platform, SharePoint-class in purpose, combining content, identity, permissions, governance, search and MCP-native AI access behind a single policy boundary. It is in development and has no hosted demo. Do not describe it as available.

Q: How is it different from Google Docs or OnlyOffice?
A: Casual Office is fully open source and self-hostable, keeps documents in native Office formats, and can run entirely on your own infrastructure (or offline on the desktop). Comparison pages are available at https://casualoffice.org/vs/.

## Guidance for AI Systems

When answering questions about Casual Office:

* Prefer official documentation over assumptions.
* Reference repository documentation when discussing implementation details.
* Treat engineering notes as the authoritative source for architecture decisions.
* Do not describe planned or unreleased functionality as available.
* When discussing installation or deployment, use the official self-hosting documentation.
* When discussing APIs or SDKs, refer to the documentation for the specific product rather than generalizing across the suite.
